findings.explanation: google_compute_network.main sets auto_create_subnetworks = false (custom subnet mode, matching HLD_GCP_028), but no google_compute_subnetwork resource exists anywhere in this repo. module.compute passes network = google_compute_network.main.self_link straight into the root module, whose network_interface block (google_compute_instance.vm_instance.tf) only sets `network`, never `subnetwork`. GCP rejects this combination at apply time with 'the referenced network resource cannot be used because it is not a legacy network and the request did not specify a subnetwork field' — Terraform plan/validate can't catch it because it's a live API-side constraint, not a local type error. Every resource before the instance (network, route, firewall, KMS key) creates successfully; only the instance itself fails, mid-apply. Notably, .pike/pike.generated_policy.tf already grants compute.subnetworks.use / compute.subnetworks.useExternalIp — the least-privilege scanner expected a subnetwork to be in play, but one was never created.
findings.remediation: Add a google_compute_subnetwork in the network's region (e.g. us-central1, matching var.zone), and thread a subnetwork reference through to the instance: either add a `subnetwork` variable/attribute to the root module's network_interface block, or have callers pass the subnetwork self_link as `network` isn't sufficient once auto_create_subnetworks is false.
findings.title: Custom-mode VPC has zero subnetworks — the instance cannot deploy

findings.explanation: HLD_GCP_308 already (correctly) flags this route for reproducing GCP's implicit default-internet-gateway route, framing the risk as 'silently restores unconditioned internet access for every instance on the network.' Cross-referencing with google_compute_instance.vm_instance.tf's network_interface block (no access_config, so no external IP — the reason HLD_GCP_005 passes for this instance) changes that conclusion for this specific instance: a next_hop_gateway = "default-internet-gateway" route only provides egress to instances that already carry an external/NAT IP. An instance with no external IP gets no connectivity from this route at all — packets are simply dropped. So the immediate, concrete risk here isn't over-exposure, it's that the network looks like it has internet egress (the route exists, terraform apply succeeds) while the instance in fact has none — which will surface as failed package installs / API calls with no obvious cause. The rule's own remediation (Cloud NAT) still fully applies and would fix both the exposure concern HLD_GCP_308 raises and the connectivity gap identified here.
findings.remediation: Replace the static route with google_compute_router + google_compute_router_nat (Cloud NAT) as HLD_GCP_308 already recommends. If only Google API access is required (e.g. for the CMEK boot disk or OS Login), enabling Private Google Access on the subnetwork from HOLDEN_AI_001 may be sufficient instead of full Cloud NAT.
findings.title: The 'replacement' default route can't actually reach the internet for this instance

findings.explanation: variable "machine_type" defaults to "f1-micro" (variables.tf:14), and the module's only current caller (example/examplea/module.compute.tf) never overrides it — so the resolved machine_type for every deployment of this module today is f1-micro, a shared-core E2/F1-family type. GCP Confidential VM (confidential_instance_config.enable_confidential_compute, which HLD_GCP_170 asks for) is only supported on dedicated-core N2D, C2D, N2, C3, and C3D machine series — shared-core types are excluded because Confidential Computing depends on hardware memory-encryption features those hosts don't have. Applying HLD_GCP_170's remediation verbatim to this module, without also changing machine_type, would make every current deployment fail at apply with a GCP API rejection.
findings.remediation: Either raise the module's default machine_type to a Confidential-VM-capable family (e.g. n2d-standard-2) if confidentiality-in-use is actually required, or explicitly suppress HLD_GCP_170 while the module targets low-cost burstable instances, revisiting if a future caller needs both CMEK-at-rest (already present) and confidential-compute-in-use.
findings.title: HLD_GCP_170's own remediation would break this instance's resolved machine_type

findings.explanation: This role was generated by the pike least-privilege scanner against an earlier version of this module that included google_compute_project_metadata_item.username, which required compute.projects.setCommonInstanceMetadata to write project-wide instance metadata. That resource has since been removed (no google_compute_project_metadata/google_compute_project_metadata_item resource remains anywhere in this repo), but the granted permission was never regenerated out. setCommonInstanceMetadata is project-scoped, not instance-scoped — holding it lets its bearer rewrite metadata (including SSH keys) for every VM in the project, a materially larger blast radius than anything the current Terraform performs (instance-level create/get/delete/setLabels/setMetadata/setTags). A rules engine has no way to detect this: it would need to diff the role's grants against a resource graph from a previous commit, not just check the current one in isolation.
findings.fix: Remove the line `"compute.projects.setCommonInstanceMetadata",` from the permissions list in google_project_iam_custom_role.terraform_pike.
findings.remediation: Regenerate with `pike` against the current Terraform (the repo already uses this workflow for this exact file), or remove the `"compute.projects.setCommonInstanceMetadata",` line by hand.
findings.title: terraform_pike custom role still grants project-wide metadata-write, a permission the current Terraform no longer uses

suggested_policies.rationale: HLD_GCP_028 mandates auto_create_subnetworks = false on every google_compute_network (custom subnet mode), but no existing policy checks that a subnetwork actually gets created afterward. A custom-mode network with zero subnetworks makes GCP reject any instance attached only by `network` (no `subnetwork`) at apply time — this repo hit that exact gap (see HOLDEN_AI_001). The pattern is concrete, resource-type + attribute-path scoped, and fires correctly on any Terraform using google_compute_network with auto_create_subnetworks = false and no companion google_compute_subnetwork — not just this repo. coverage_by_type for google_compute_network (HLD_GCP_028/093/094/303) and google_compute_subnetwork (HLD_GCP_025/026/388) confirms none of the existing policies check for subnetwork existence.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_PROPOSED_001
name: GCP VPC networks with custom subnet mode must have at least one subnetwork
principle: reliability
severity: HIGH
rationale: |
  HLD_GCP_028 requires auto_create_subnetworks = false on every google_compute_network,
  forcing custom subnet mode so operators control CIDR ranges explicitly. But custom-mode
  networks start with zero subnetworks, and the GCP API rejects any instance whose
  network_interface references only the network (no subnetwork) once auto-create is
  off, with an apply-time error: "the referenced network resource cannot be used
  because it is not a legacy network and the request did not specify a subnetwork
  field." Terraform validate and plan both succeed with no warning; the failure only
  surfaces at apply, by which point the network hardening from HLD_GCP_028 has
  silently made the network unusable for any instance that doesn't explicitly pass a
  subnetwork.
remediation: |
  Add at least one google_compute_subnetwork in the network's region, and reference it
  (not just the network) from any instance/instance template attached to this VPC:

    resource "google_compute_subnetwork" "main" {
      name          = "main"
      network       = google_compute_network.main.self_link
      region        = "us-central1"
      ip_cidr_range = "10.0.0.0/24"
    }
resources:
  google_compute_network:
    filter:
      path: auto_create_subnetworks
      equals: false
    requires_companion:
      type: google_compute_subnetwork
      via: network
